newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean parliament grills president's son.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean parliament grills president's son.

text.p: The son of South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Friday appeared for questioning at a televised parliamentary hearing into a multi-billion dollar corporate loans scandal.
Kim Hyun-chul, 38, the second son of the beleaguered president, was ushered in to the National Assembly wearing a dark grey business suit to give sworn testimony.
Lawmakers said before the hearing they would grill him over allegations he took a big pay-off in a deal involving the failed Hanbo Steel Co at the centre of the scandal.
He bowed deeply before taking his place behind a microphone on a bench in the chamber.
Shortly after lawmakers began their questioning, the younger Kim apologised to the South Korean public and to his father for causing a "furore".
President Kim has also apologised on television over the loan scandal and the behaviour of his son, who has become one his biggest political liabilities.
Political analysts said the son's testimony could further weaken the authority of the president, who has already become a lame duck in his last year of office.

State prosecutors have been delving into allegations that Kim Hyun-chul took a 200 billion won ($224 million) kickback from a businessman acting as an agent for Hanbo. The businessman has denied the charges.
Kim Hyun-chul denied on Friday he meddled in appointments of senior officials, although he recommended some people to his father.
"When my father asked me, I just recommended widely respected and outstanding people," he said.
He also denied rumours he had asked the founder of Hanbo Group, Chung Tae-woo, to launder some of the money he allegedly kept from the funds left over from his father's 1992 presidential campaign.
Kim Hyun-chul played an important role in the campaign, and opposition lawmakers have said they would question him over whether he kept some of the unspent campaign funds.
"I believe I must be punished if I committed crime," Kim Hyun-chul said. But asked if he thought he had violated laws, he said: "I don't think so."

South Korean people have been riveted by the scandal that erupted after Hanbo Steel, South Korea's second largest steelmaker, collapsed in January under debts of $5.8 billion, a large chunk of them without collateral.
The scandal revealed sleazy links between businessmen, politicians and bankers despite the president's widely published drive to root out corruption.
Hanbo founder Chung is standing trial for corruption along with nine other people, including a former cabinet minister, close associates of the president, politicians and bankers.
Prosecutors have said politicians pressured banks to keep loans rolling into Hanbo in return for kickbacks.
A prosecution official said Park Tae-jung, a businessman suspected of managing money for the president's son, was to be questioned by prosecutors in the Hanbo case.

Police last month raided Park's home and offices. They confiscated boxes of papers and computer discs as part of their investigation into opposition charges that Park, acting as an agent for Hanbo, funnelled money to the president's son in return for help in securing loans.
